summary: Nike's fiscal first-quarter 2024 revenue of $12.94 billion narrowly missed the $12.98 billion estimate, the first revenue miss in two years, but EPS of 94 cents and a 44.2% gross margin beat expectations, sending shares up about 8% after hours. Growth came from direct sales, Europe and footwear, while North America, Converse and apparel were weak and China fell short of estimates. Management kept full-year guidance and cautioned about holiday demand, markdowns and student loan payments resuming.
one_line: Nike missed Q1 fiscal 2024 revenue estimates for the first time in two years but beat on earnings and gross margin, lifting its shares about 8%.
key_facts: Nike reported fiscal Q1 revenue of $12.94 billion vs. $12.98 billion expected by LSEG, its first revenue miss in two years; sales were up about 2% from $12.69 billion a year earlier.
Nike's earnings per share were 94 cents vs. 75 cents expected; net income was $1.45 billion vs. $1.47 billion a year earlier.
Nike shares rose about 8% in extended trading on Thursday.
Gross margin fell about 0.1 percentage points to 44.2%, but beat the 43.7% StreetAccount estimate; higher product costs and currency rates were offset by price increases.

Nike maintained full-year guidance of mid-single-digit revenue growth and gross margin expansion of 1.4 to 1.6 percentage points; for Q2 it expects slightly higher revenue and about 1 percentage point of gross margin growth.
China sales grew 5% to $1.7 billion, short of the $1.8 billion analysts expected; the prior quarter had seen a 16% jump against easy Covid-lockdown comparisons.
North America sales fell 2% to $5.42 billion; EMEA rose 8% to $3.61 billion; Latin America and Asia Pacific rose 2% to $1.57 billion.
Converse sales were $588 million, down 9% and well short of the roughly $660 million expected, a second quarter in a row of falling short.
Nike's direct channel grew 6%, with store traffic up double digits; wholesale revenue was flat at $7 billion.
Nike restored its relationships with Macy's and DSW, praised Dick's Sporting Goods, and is still resetting its business with Footlocker.
Footwear sales rose 4% to $8.4 billion (about 68% of total sales) while apparel fell 1% to $3.4 billion.
A Jefferies survey found 54% of respondents plan to spend less on apparel and accessories and 46% less on footwear; student loan payments resume in October.
